newsitem.title: UK: Bond markets typically shine in Nov-Dec -analysts.
newsitem.headline: Bond markets typically shine in Nov-Dec -analysts.

text.p: If the past is anything to go by, investors would make money by buying bonds in the run up to Christmas, analysts said.
Whatever the reason, bonds around the world have tended to rally during November and December for most of the past decade -- a trend which has hardly been lost on market-watchers.
"It's definately true. You always see it," said Brian Venables, senior bond strategist at ABN-Amro Hoare Govett.
Venables and others suggested a host of explanations, ranging from typical year-end "window dressing" to more concrete factors such as the lack of fresh supply during this period.
Yet this is also one of the more illiquid times of the year and they said investors could hardly bank on profiting by the apparent seasonal tug on debt markets.
According to Norman Beauchamp, head of derivatives at Cooperative Bank in London, bonds have rallied in nine of the past 10 years in November and December, led by U.S. Treasuries.
He suggested window dressing, where investors buy high-flying securities so their year-end books look attractive.
"People try to pretty up their books for the end of the year," Beauchamp said. "Christmas euphoria also tends to boost the market higher."
So why are people not snapping up bonds at this time of year, simply on the view that they can reap short-term gains?
"Theoretically you could do that, and nine times out of 10 you'd make profits," said Venables, based in Amsterdam.
But fund managers said they cared far more about fundamental factors than such historical trends, and were more concerned about choosing their portfolio for the next year.
And for the trading community, many dealers grow conservative as the end of the year approaches as they do not want to jeopardise their upcoming bonuses.
"Everyone gets very risk averse towards the end of the year. If you've made profits why risk them?" Venables said. "If you've had a bad year, why make it worse?"

On the more concrete side, he said supply factors were in bonds' favour as Christmas approached. Analysts said authorities tended not to hold bond auctions during this period as markets were usually quiet.
"You really don't have the supply and demand pressures on the market that you get in the rest of the year. That all seems to result in a rather bullish atmosphere," Venables said.

Economic policy decisions are more likely to favour bond markets during the season as well, some said. If they had a choice, central banks would put off any unpopular interest rate decisions right before Christmas, they said.
"From an interest rate perspective, if the Fed is going to do anything, it's certainly not going to do it in December," said Kirit Shah, chief market strategist at Sanwa International in London.
So far, T-bonds have been acting according to script.
The December T-bond futures were at 115-21 at 1320 GMT, up from 113-01 at the start of November.
"I'm looking for T-bonds to get to 116-00 and that should drag the other markets higher," Beauchamp said.
Shah and Venables said 1994 was one time when bonds failed to rally in November and December, but they had been bearish throughout the year leading up to those two months.
Fund managers remain sceptical about the trend.
For those who are already long on bonds going into the end of the year, the seasonal factor -- if it in fact exists -- is just an added attraction, not a reason to take new positions.
"Of course, it's a bonus for us," said Kim Thomsen, head of fixed income at Danske Invest in Copenhagen, Denmark's largest unit trust fund with $2.5 billion.

Yet Paul Meader, haed of fixed-income at Matheson Investment management in Guernsey, said trying to chase the trend would be a real mistake. "Anybody who invests on the basis of past trends in investments is going to lose money."
